description: a when handler delivered by the HOST, through the tick dispatcher, is charged exactly like one fired synchronously at registration. when has two delivery paths - the direct invokeWhenHandler call executeWhenStatement makes for the immediate "start" fire, and the tick drain for host-delivered named events - and when-firing-counts-against-budget only exercises the first, so charging one but not the other passed the whole corpus. The empty body makes the firing the only chargeable thing: the registration, the wait statement, and its single now-charged tick consume the budget of 3 exactly, so the pause itself completes and the handler's own firing is the instruction that cannot be afforded. An implementation that charged only the registration-time path completes this program cleanly -- measured, not asserted: with the host event removed so no firing can occur, this program at budget 3 runs clean in 4 events, while the same program written with `wait 4` still raises ol-limit at the `wait` on its second tick. That is why the pause is one tick and not four: before issue #953 made a `wait` tick a charged instruction the count did not matter, but at budget 3 a longer pause exhausts the budget on its own and the stated control becomes false, leaving the fixture halting for the right reason while asserting a discrimination it no longer performs. The recorded event stream is byte-identical under either spelling; only the control's truth differs
